title: The New Science of Naples: the Ladder, the Chair, and the Nations
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Via San Biagio dei Librai, the room above the shop
stops.campa: Giambattista is born in a small room above his father Antonio's bookshop, on the street of the booksellers that cuts the old Greek city in a straight line, shelves of leather spines rising from the counter below to the ceiling of his birth. His father is a Neapolitan bookseller of a lively wit; his mother, Candida Masullo, a coachbuilder's daughter. The house stands among the palazzi and cloisters of the ancient center, closer to print and paper than to rank or fortune, which is exactly the inheritance the child will spend a lifetime turning into philosophy.
suggested_refs: The commemorative plaque at Via San Biagio dei Librai, Naples: 'In questa cameretta nacque il XXIII giugno MDCLXVIII Giambattista Vico'
sources: Vico, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo (1725-1731)
Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)

stops.name: The church of San Gennaro all'Olmo, the baptism
stops.campa: Two days after his birth the infant is carried the short distance from the bookshop to the parish church of San Gennaro all'Olmo, at the corner where the street of the booksellers meets the street of the plaster-crib makers, and is given the name Giambattista at the font. The Naples he is born into is a viceregal city of the Spanish crown, dense with churches, monasteries, and the din of a hundred trades in a few hundred meters of lava-stone streets; this parish, this font, this crossing of two narrow ways will remain the fixed center of his whole geography.
suggested_refs: The parish church of San Gennaro all'Olmo, at the corner of Via San Biagio dei Librai and Via San Gregorio Armeno
sources: Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)
Naples parish and neighborhood histories, Via San Biagio dei Librai

stops.name: The fall from the ladder
stops.campa: At seven years old the boy falls headlong from the top of a high ladder in his father's shop and lies on the stone floor for five hours without sense or motion. The fall breaks the right side of his skull; a great tumor rises over the fracture. The surgeon, sounding the wound, tells the family plainly that the child will either die of it or, living, grow up an idiot. Neither comes to pass. He recovers slowly, and marks this fall ever after as the hinge on which his whole nature turned: the accident that made the philosopher.
suggested_refs: Vico's own account of the fall, opening pages of the Vita, cited in nearly every modern biography
sources: Vico, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo
Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)

stops.name: Three years mending: the shop becomes a school
stops.campa: For three years the recovering boy is kept from ordinary schooling, sickly, slow, and given to long silences among the bound volumes of his father's stock. He teaches himself to read early and widely, alone among the shelves, before he can properly be said to have been taught by anyone. Of this convalescence Vico will later say that it left him a natural melancholy and a quick temper, the very temper, he insists, that belongs to men of ingenuity and depth of mind: the wound is not an injury to be regretted but the first mark of a vocation.
suggested_refs: The bookshop of Antonio Vico, Via San Biagio dei Librai, as described in the opening of the Vita
sources: Vico, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo
Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)

segments.name: The Grammar Schools and the Silence

stops.name: The Jesuit classes and the broken lesson
stops.campa: Sent to the Jesuit schools at the Collegio del Salvatore, beside the church of the Gesù Vecchio, to learn grammar and the syllogism, the boy is placed in a lower class than he believes he has earned, quarrels with the master over the demotion, and walks out of the schoolroom, finishing the course at home. It is a small schoolboy's rupture, and it changes everything: from this day the shape of his mind is his own to build, unsupervised, out of whatever books the shop and his own hunger supply, rather than out of any syllabus set by other men.
suggested_refs: The Collegio del Salvatore, beside the church of the Gesù Vecchio on Via Giovanni Paladino, seat of the Neapolitan Jesuit schools of Vico's boyhood
sources: Vico, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo
Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)

stops.name: Self-teaching: the Scholastics abandoned, law read alone
stops.campa: Left to himself, the youth reads without a master's order: scholastic logic first, which soon disgusts him with its dry disputations; then, ranging further, the civil law, some geometry, and whatever poets and historians pass over his father's counter. He confesses later that he never mastered geometry's neat method to his own satisfaction and never regretted it, since the mathematical proof, so prized by the new philosophy of his century, seemed to him to teach the mind certainty about dead abstractions while leaving it blind to the living, changing world of men, laws, and nations it would spend a life explaining.
suggested_refs: Vico's later polemic against Cartesian 'clear and distinct ideas' as a standard for the human sciences, De nostri temporis studiorum ratione (1708)
sources: Vico, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo
Vico, De nostri temporis studiorum ratione (1709)

stops.name: Arrival at the castle of the Rocca, Vatolla
stops.campa: At eighteen Vico rides south out of Naples into the Cilento, a hundred kilometers down the coast, to become tutor to the nephews of the bishop of Ischia in the family castle at Vatolla, a stronghold of cylindrical towers above the hill-town's narrow streets. He expects a few years of quiet employment; he stays nine. The court's business, the city's noise, the competitions and patronages of the capital, all recede behind him; what remains is a schoolroom, two boys to instruct in grammar and letters, and, waiting behind an unlocked door down the corridor, the richest private library he has yet seen.
suggested_refs: The Palazzo Vargas (Castello di Vatolla), now housing the Centro di Studi Vichiani and a Vico museum and library
sources: Vico, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo
Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)

stops.name: The castle library: the four authors
stops.campa: In the castle's library and the books of the nearby convent of Santa Maria della Pietà, undisturbed by the fashions of the capital, Vico reads for the first time the four authors he will name for the rest of his life as the makers of his mind: Plato, for an eternal justice above positive law; Tacitus, for what men actually do rather than what philosophers say they should; Francis Bacon, for the ideal of a science still to be founded; and Hugo Grotius, for the whole compass of a jurisprudence of nations. Out of these four, in a provincial hill town, the New Science is already being assembled.
suggested_refs: Vico's list of his 'four authors' (Plato, Tacitus, Bacon, Grotius), recurring across the Vita and the Scienza Nuova
The convent library of Santa Maria della Pietà at Vatolla, the other reading room of the tutorship years
sources: Vico, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo
Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)

stops.name: News from Naples: the trial of the freethinkers
stops.campa: Word reaches the castle of a tribunal convened in Naples against a circle of young physicians and philosophers charged with holding impious, Epicurean, and atheistic opinions drawn from the new mechanist science. Vico, tutoring by day and reading Plato and Tacitus by candle at night, marks the lesson without needing to be told it twice: a natural philosophy that explains away providence, and a jurisprudence built on force alone, both end at the same cliff-edge. Whatever system he builds afterward will insist on divine providence working through, not against, the free and often violent doings of men and nations.
suggested_refs: The 1688 Neapolitan trial of the 'atei' (freethinking physicians and philosophers), a formative episode of Vico's intellectual generation
sources: Vico, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo
Naples intellectual history of the 1680s, the Investiganti circle and its aftermath

stops.name: The doctorate in civil and canon law
stops.campa: Vico rides back from Vatolla to sit and pass his examinations, taking the doctorate in civil and canon law that his schoolroom quarrel had interrupted years before. Whether the degree was conferred at Naples or, as his editors suspect, at Salerno is disputed to this day. It is a formality set beside the education the castle has actually given him, but it is the credential the world outside Vatolla will ask to see: the parchment that lets a bookseller's self-taught son call himself, before notaries and future employers, a doctor of laws, and so stand for the chairs he will chase ever after.
suggested_refs: Vico's doctorate in utroque iure, c. 1693-94; the conferring university (Naples or Salerno) is disputed in the scholarship
sources: Vico, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo
Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)

stops.name: Return to Naples
stops.campa: After nine years the tutorship ends and Vico comes back down out of the Cilento hills to his father's city for good, carrying in his head the library of Vatolla rather than in his hands: Plato, Tacitus, Bacon, Grotius, and a store of Latin and Italian poetry read in solitude. He is twenty-seven, unbeneficed, unmarried, without patron or post, a doctor of laws with no chair to fill it, returning to the same narrow streets of booksellers and notaries he left as a boy, to begin the slow, underpaid climb through which the whole of his mature thought will be produced.
suggested_refs: Naples, the old center around Via San Biagio dei Librai and Via dei Tribunali, Vico's working world for the rest of his life
sources: Vico, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo
Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)

stops.name: The competition for the chair of eloquence
stops.campa: At the Palazzo dei Regi Studi, the royal university housed in the great barracks-turned-college above the old city, Vico competes for and wins the chair of rhetoric, professor of Latin eloquence, a post that pays badly and carries little honor beside the coveted chair of civil law he really wants. He will hold it, nonetheless, for forty-two years. That October he opens the academic year with the first of his inaugural orations, and the bookseller's self-taught son stands at a lectern in the hall of the Studi to teach the sons of Naples how to speak well and, he already suspects, how to think.
suggested_refs: The Palazzo dei Regi Studi, seat of the University of Naples from 1616, now the Museo Archeologico Nazionale
sources: Vico, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo
Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)

stops.name: Marriage to Teresa Caterina Destito
stops.campa: In the same year as his chair, Vico marries Teresa Caterina Destito, a childhood friend of the neighborhood, unlettered but, he will say, of a strength and good sense that carried the household through poverty he could never fully lift with a rhetorician's stipend. Eight children follow across the years, not all of whom survive childhood, and hardship visits the household more than once before the end. Of the household's daily arithmetic, pawned rings and unpaid rents against the price of paper and print, Vico says almost nothing directly in his own account; the New Science, when it comes, will be paid for out of exactly this scarcity.
suggested_refs: Vico's household in the old center of Naples, described piecemeal across the Vita and his correspondence
sources: Vico, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo
Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)

stops.name: The annual orations: teaching the young of Naples
stops.campa: Each October, opening the academic year, the professor of eloquence delivers before the assembled students of the Studi a formal oration on the aims of study and the good life of the mind: six of these survive from his first years in the chair, urging the young toward a wisdom that joins eloquence to virtue and knowledge to civic use, against the narrow specialist who knows much and understands little. Vico is, by his own account, a poor and hesitant public speaker, plain rather than polished, and yet these annual addresses to the students of Naples become, oration by oration, the workshop in which his whole philosophy of education and history is first hammered into shape.
suggested_refs: Vico's six Orazioni inaugurali (Inaugural Orations), 1699-1707, delivered at the opening of the academic year; the seventh is De nostri temporis studiorum ratione
sources: Vico, Orazioni inaugurali
Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)

stops.name: De nostri temporis studiorum ratione
stops.campa: On the eighteenth of October, marking the university's formal reopening, Vico delivers his seventh and most consequential inaugural oration, On the Study Methods of Our Time. Against the reigning Cartesian fashion, which prizes the geometrical method and the critical faculty above all, he argues for the older art of topics, the training of memory, imagination, and a quick sense of the probable and the concrete, without which no student ever learns prudence, eloquence, or the capacity to judge particular human affairs. The mathematical method that sharpens judgment about lines and numbers, he warns his audience, can atrophy the very faculties that govern courts, cities, and nations.
suggested_refs: De nostri temporis studiorum ratione (1708, published 1709), Vico's seventh inaugural oration
sources: Vico, De nostri temporis studiorum ratione (1709)
Wikipedia, De nostri temporis studiorum ratione

stops.name: De antiquissima Italorum sapientia: verum ipsum factum
stops.campa: Working alone in Naples on the etymologies of the old Italic tongues, Vico publishes the first part of a metaphysics he means to found on the wisdom buried in the Latin language itself, and states there, in four Latin words, the axiom the whole New Science will be built upon: the true and the made are convertible. Only the maker of a thing can fully know it; God alone truly knows nature, which He made, while men can truly know only what men themselves have made, which is history, language, law, and the civil world of nations. The axiom sounds abstract; it will turn out to be the key to everything that follows.
suggested_refs: The 1710 first edition of De antiquissima Italorum sapientia, title page and opening chapter on verum-factum
sources: Vico, De antiquissima Italorum sapientia (1710)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giambattista Vico'

segments.name: Il Diritto Universale and the Defeat

stops.name: De uno universi juris principio et fine uno
stops.campa: Still hoping to be called at last to the chair of civil law, Vico publishes the first volume of a projected universal jurisprudence, arguing that all positive law, however various among the nations, descends from one single principle and aims at one single end: the justice that providence works into human affairs across time, whether men know it or not. It is a lawyer's treatise built like a metaphysics and a metaphysics built like a history of law; readers accustomed to ordinary legal commentary do not know quite what shelf to put it on, and the book that was meant to win him a chair wins him instead a narrower and stranger readership.
suggested_refs: De uno universi juris principio et fine uno (1720), first volume of Il Diritto Universale
sources: Vico, De uno universi juris principio et fine uno (1720)
Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)

stops.name: De constantia iurisprudentis
stops.campa: A second volume follows, De constantia iurisprudentis, in which Vico turns from the single principle of law to the constancy of the jurist's own judgment across the changes of nations: how a Roman praetor, a feudal baron's magistrate, and a modern Neapolitan judge can all be said to practice one continuous art of equity, though the customs, weapons, and languages around them are unrecognizable from one age to the next. The three ages he will later name gods, heroes, and men are already visible here, half-formed, moving beneath the technical apparatus of a lawbook few outside Naples will ever read.
suggested_refs: De constantia iurisprudentis (1721), second volume of Il Diritto Universale
sources: Vico, De constantia iurisprudentis (1721)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giambattista Vico'

stops.name: The Notae, the third volume closes the work
stops.campa: Vico closes Il Diritto Universale with a volume of Notae, annotations and clarifications answering objections and tightening the argument of the two books before it, a scholar's habit of returning to correct and complete rather than simply moving on to the next title. He is fifty-four, three heavy Latin volumes deep into a case for the chair he covets, and still without it. The books have cost him money he cannot easily spare and bought him a small circle of admirers in the Republic of Letters, but not, so far, the one appointment that would let him teach what he actually believes.
suggested_refs: Notae in duos libros (1722), closing the three-part Diritto Universale
sources: Vico, Notae in duos libros (1722)
Peter Harrington Books, catalogue note on the 1722 Notae

stops.name: The competition for the chair of civil law, lost
stops.campa: The morning chair of civil law falls vacant at last and Vico competes for it before the assembled Studi, certain that three published volumes of jurisprudence must weigh more than rivals with better family connections and no comparable body of work. He has no patron in the vice-regal government; the post goes to Domenico Gentile. It is the bitterest disappointment of his professional life, and, by his own later account, the hinge of his second and greater turn: robbed of the career he wanted, he sits down instead to gather everything he has read and thought, at Vatolla and after, into a single new science of nations.
suggested_refs: The 1723 competition (24 March and 24 April) for the morning chair of civil law at the University of Naples, won by Domenico Gentile
sources: Vico, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo
Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)

stops.name: The ring sold, the first Scienza Nuova printed
stops.campa: Unable to find a patron willing to underwrite the printing, Vico sells his one gold ring to pay the press, and the Principj di una Scienza Nuova intorno alla natura delle nazioni appears in Naples in a modest, badly funded edition: the discovery, he announces, of a new science of the common nature of nations, built on the axiom that men can truly know only the civil world they themselves have made. He sends copies out to scholars across Italy and beyond, hoping for the recognition Naples has withheld; most of the learned world does not yet know what to do with it.
suggested_refs: The 1725 first edition of the Scienza Nuova (Principj di una Scienza Nuova intorno alla natura delle nazioni)
sources: Vico, Principj di una Scienza Nuova (1725)
Vico, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo

stops.name: Poetic wisdom: the first men, children of the world
stops.campa: At the heart of the new science stands its strangest and most fertile claim: the first men of the gentile nations, unable yet to reason abstractly, thought in bodies and passions, imagining thunder as an angry god and the sky itself as a great animated body watching them; this poetic wisdom, sapienza poetica, is not primitive error to be outgrown but the very faculty, the imaginative universal, out of which law, religion, and language are first made. The nations do not begin with philosophers. They begin, every one of them, as poets who do not yet know they are speaking in metaphor.
suggested_refs: Vico's doctrine of sapienza poetica (poetic wisdom) and the imaginative universal, Book Two of the Scienza Nuova
sources: Vico, Scienza Nuova (1725, 1730, 1744)
Isaiah Berlin, Vico and Herder (1976)

stops.name: The three ages: gods, heroes, and men
stops.campa: Out of the study of Rome, of the Greeks, of the barbarian kingdoms after the fall of empire, and of his own Naples, Vico draws the pattern he believes governs every nation without exception: an age of gods, in which oracles and rites rule savage families through fear of the divine; an age of heroes, in which a warrior nobility holds law and land against the common people by force dressed as custom; and an age of men, in which reason, equality, and written law finally prevail, until the nation, grown too rational and too soft, falls back toward a new barbarism and the cycle turns again.
suggested_refs: The doctrine of the tre età (three ages) of gods, heroes, and men, central table of the Scienza Nuova
sources: Vico, Scienza Nuova (1725, 1730, 1744)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giambattista Vico'

stops.name: The Second New Science and the dipintura
stops.campa: Vico rewrites the whole work almost from the ground up for a second edition, clearer in argument and richer in the philology of Homer, Roman law, and the feudal chronicles, and opens it with an emblematic frontispiece, the dipintura, designed with his Neapolitan friend the sculptor Domenico Antonio Vaccaro: a ray from the eye of divine providence striking the breast of metaphysics, a broken statue of Homer, the instruments of the nations' arts arranged around a globe. He spends eighty pages explaining, image by image, what the engraving means, insisting that the whole science can be read, compressed, in that single sheet before a single sentence of prose.
suggested_refs: The dipintura, allegorical frontispiece of the 1730 Scienza Nuova, engraved after Domenico Antonio Vaccaro's design
sources: Vico, Scienza Nuova (1730), 'Spiegazione della Dipintura'
Jscholarship/JHU, 'Through a Jewel, Darkly: A Reading of the Frontispiece'

stops.name: Corsi e ricorsi: the barbarism that returns
stops.campa: Vico names the great mechanism of his history corso and ricorso: nations do not simply progress in a straight line toward reason, they run a full course from divine to heroic to human government and then, when the human age curdles into a hyper-rational, self-interested barbarism of reflection worse than the first barbarism of the senses, they collapse and recur, falling back through a new age of force before a new cycle of gods, heroes, and men can begin again. Rome's fall and Europe's feudal centuries are, on this reading, not an interruption of history but history's own recurring grammar, read correctly for the first time.
suggested_refs: The doctrine of corsi e ricorsi (courses and recourses) and the barbarie della riflessione, Book Five of the Scienza Nuova
sources: Vico, Scienza Nuova (1730, 1744), Book Five, 'Ricorso'
Isaiah Berlin, Vico and Herder (1976)

stops.name: De mente heroica: the oration on the heroic mind
stops.campa: Opening the academic year at the Studi, the aging professor delivers his oration De mente heroica, calling on the young men before him to unfold within themselves a heroic mind, a greatness of soul that seeks not private gain but the good of the whole human race, and to put every art and science they study, however specialized, in that mind's service. It is Vico's own answer, spoken aloud to a hall of students, to a Cartesian age he thinks trains clever calculators and produces very few heroes; the lecture is, in miniature, everything his New Science hopes the nations of men might yet become.
suggested_refs: De mente heroica (1732), Vico's oration to the students of the University of Naples, 20 October 1732
sources: Vico, De mente heroica (1732)
Silvia Ruffo Fiore, 'Giambattista Vico and the Pedagogy of Heroic Mind'

stops.name: Count Porcia's invitation
stops.campa: For some years the count Gian Artico di Porcìa has been circulating among the learned men of Italy a proposal, his Progetto ai letterati d'Italia: that each set down, for the instruction of the young, the story of how he came to think as he thinks, a scholar's autobiography written not to flatter but to teach. Vico, poor, provincial, still stung by the lost chair, answers the call and begins, in the same year the first Scienza Nuova goes to press, to compose the story of his own mind's formation, from the fall on the ladder to the axiom that the true and the made are one.
suggested_refs: Count Gian Artico di Porcìa's 1725 circular inviting Italian scholars to write philosophical autobiographies
sources: Vico, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo
Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)

stops.name: The Vita begun, written in the third person
stops.campa: Vico writes his life not as I but as he, following the model of the physician Girolamo Cardano's own strange autobiography, narrating Giambattista Vico's birth, fall, schooling, and reading as if reporting on another man observed from outside, a philosopher's case history of himself. The device lets him treat his own melancholic temperament, his slow self-education, and his defeats in the university competitions as data for a general science of how minds like his are made, rather than as private grievance: the same instinct that will let him read the myths of whole peoples as true, dependable evidence of how nations think.
suggested_refs: The third-person narration of the Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo, modeled on Girolamo Cardano's autobiography
sources: Vico, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo
Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)

stops.name: The first part published in Calogerà's Raccolta
stops.campa: The first part of the Vita appears at Venice in the opening volume of the Raccolta d'opuscoli scientifici e filologici, the anthology begun that year by the Camaldolese monk Angelo Calogerà, printed in the same volume as Porcìa's own Progetto that had asked for it. Vico's account stands out among its companion lives for its philosophical ambition, tracing not just a career but the genesis of an entire new science out of one man's reading, poverty, and disappointments. Few readers outside a narrow circle notice it at the time; a much later century will recognize the Vita as one of the first true philosophical autobiographies in Europe.
suggested_refs: Raccolta d'opuscoli scientifici e filologici, vol. 1 (Venice, 1728), ed. Angelo Calogerà, containing Porcìa's Progetto and the first published part of Vico's Vita
sources: Vico, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo (1728)
Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)

stops.name: The continuation added
stops.campa: Vico adds a continuation carrying the story forward through the second Scienza Nuova and his ongoing quarrel with rivals and reviewers who mock his obscurity or accuse him of stealing from Grotius and Bacon the very authors he has always openly named as his teachers. He will keep adding notes and corrections to his own life almost until the year of his death, a scholar's habit turned autobiographical: the Vita, like the New Science it explains, is never quite finished, only left off at whatever point the pen, or the life, runs out.
suggested_refs: The 1731 continuation of the Vita, carrying the account through the second Scienza Nuova
sources: Vico, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo
Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)

segments.name: Historiographer Royal and the Silent Bier

stops.name: Historiographer royal to the new king
stops.campa: Charles of Bourbon, the young king who has just carried Naples out of Austrian rule into an independent crown, names Vico historiographer royal, a title that comes with a salary larger than a lifetime's rhetoric chair ever paid and almost no duties attached to it. At the Palazzo Reale, the honor Vico never quite won through the university's own competitions arrives instead by royal favor, late, a little beside the point, and welcome anyway: a court title for a professor who has spent his career teaching eloquence to the sons of lawyers while quietly rewriting the history of every nation that ever told a myth about itself.
suggested_refs: Palazzo Reale di Napoli, seat of Charles of Bourbon's new independent Kingdom of Naples from 1734
sources: Vico, Vita di Giambattista Vico scritta da se medesimo (continuations)
Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)

stops.name: Retirement; the chair passes to his son
stops.campa: Failing health, deafness, and the weight of over forty years at the lectern finally force Vico to give up the chair of rhetoric at the Studi. It passes, by his own arrangement and the university's consent, to his son Gennaro, himself trained in the family discipline of letters and law. The bookseller's grandson now teaches where the bookseller's son taught before him, in the same halls above the old city, the same annual orations to open the academic year that Vico delivered as a young, hopeful, overlooked competitor for a post he had once considered beneath him.
suggested_refs: Gennaro Vico, successor to his father's chair of rhetoric at the University of Naples, 1741
sources: Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giambattista Vico'

stops.name: Death, 23 January 1744
stops.campa: Giambattista Vico dies in Naples at seventy-five, in the same old quarter of booksellers and notaries where he was born, having buried children of his own and spent a life mostly unrecognized outside a small circle for the single idea he was most sure of: that the nations of the world, in their myths, laws, and languages, hand down a true and continuous history of themselves, if only a reader learns to read it as they meant it, and not as later, more rational ages have mistranslated it into fable, error, or lie.
suggested_refs: Vico's death notice and the family's account of his final illness, appended to later editions of the Vita
sources: Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giambattista Vico'

stops.name: The silent bier: the funeral dispute
stops.campa: Two bodies claim the honor of carrying Vico's coffin to burial: the professors of the university, who count him one of their own, and the lay Confraternity of Santa Sofia, of which he was long a member. Neither will yield precedence, the quarrel turning on who is to hold the tassels of the pall, and at last both parties withdraw altogether, leaving the coffin standing unburied among the mourners. It is a scene the New Science itself might have used as evidence: rank and ceremony, in the age of men, quarreling so bitterly over their due that they forget the plain duty of burying the dead.
suggested_refs: The Marquis of Villarosa's 1818 account of the disputed funeral, appended to later editions of the Vita
sources: Marquis of Villarosa, continuation to Vico's Vita (1818)
Fisch & Bergin, The Autobiography of Giambattista Vico (1944, trans.)

stops.name: Burial in the church of the Girolamini
stops.campa: With neither the professors nor the confraternity willing to bury him, it falls at last to the canons of the cathedral to see the philosopher decently to his rest in the church of the Girolamini, on the old decumanus of the city, the Via dei Tribunali. A plaque set along the colonnade between the nave and the left aisle still names him; the old guides to Naples place the body itself in the hypogeum beneath the chapel of Sant'Agnese. It is a quieter monument by far than the reputation the New Science will eventually earn him, in a church of Oratorian priests he never belonged to.
suggested_refs: The commemorative plaque to Giambattista Vico along the colonnade of the Church of the Girolamini, Naples; the traditional burial site is the hypogeum beneath the chapel of Sant'Agnese
sources: CulturalHeritageOnline, 'Library and Monumental Complex of the Girolamini'
Naples Life, Death & Miracle, 'Giambattista Vico Foundation'

stops.name: The third Scienza Nuova, published without him
stops.campa: Later the same year, the third and final edition of the Scienza Nuova appears in Naples, the text Vico had been revising and clarifying up to his last working days, its account of the three ages and the corsi e ricorsi carried through to its fullest and most finished form. He does not live to see it bound and sold. It will lie mostly unread outside a narrow Neapolitan circle for another century, until Jules Michelet in France and, later, an even wider nineteenth- and twentieth-century readership recognize in this posthumous edition one of the founding texts of the philosophy of history.
suggested_refs: The third, posthumous 1744 edition of the Scienza Nuova, Vico's final revision
sources: Vico, Scienza Nuova (1744)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Giambattista Vico'

stops.name: Dante, the second Homer of a returned barbarism
stops.campa: Working out the New Science's long central argument on the true Homer, Vico turns his method on a poet nearer home: Dante, he judges, stands to the returned barbarism of medieval Italy exactly as Homer stood to the first heroic age of Greece, a mind of towering individual genius born, almost impossibly, out of a fierce and unlettered century, giving that raw age its first true history in verse rather than in chronicle. He warns readers of the Comedy against every moral allegory laid over it afterward: read it, he says, as the age's own reflection on itself, and it needs no gloss to be true.
suggested_refs: Vico's Giudizio sopra Dante, appended to La discoverta del vero Omero
sources: Vico, Scienza Nuova, Book Three ('Discoverta del vero Omero') and the Giudizio sopra Dante
Edizioni ETS, La discoverta del vero Omero seguita dal Giudizio sopra Dante

stops.name: The claim: myth is the true history of the nations
stops.campa: The whole New Science rests, in the end, on a single reversal of the ordinary judgment against fable: the myths every gentile nation tells of its own gods and heroes are not later poets' lies laid over a forgotten past, but the first, plain, unmetaphorical history that a people, still speaking in the only language available to it, poetic wisdom, could tell about what its own ancestors actually did and believed. Read rightly, without modern condescension, the fable is the archive; the marvel narrated is the event as its own witnesses first understood it. It is exactly the register in which every journey answering to this claim must, ever after, be told.
stops.quote: But in the night of thick darkness enveloping the earliest antiquity, so remote from ourselves, there shines the eternal and never failing light of a truth beyond all question: that the world of civil society has certainly been made by men, and that its principles are therefore to be found within the modifications of our own human mind.
suggested_refs: The founding maxim of the Scienza Nuova on the civil world as a human, knowable making
sources: Vico, Scienza Nuova (1744)
Bergin & Fisch (trans.), The New Science of Giambattista Vico (1948)

stops.name: Michelet in Paris translates the Scienza Nuova
stops.campa: In Paris, a young archivist and teacher of history named Jules Michelet reads the Neapolitan nobody has read and publishes Principes de la philosophie de l'histoire, a French rendering of the Scienza Nuova prefaced by a discourse on the system and the life of its author. It is the hinge of Vico's fortunes: from this small volume the corsi e ricorsi, the poetic wisdom, and above all the conviction that history is made by the customs and fables of ordinary people pass into French historiography, and from there into the whole nineteenth century's idea of what a people is.
suggested_refs: Jules Michelet, Principes de la philosophie de l'histoire, traduits de la Scienza nuova de J.-B. Vico (Paris, Jules Renouard, 1827); expanded as Oeuvres choisies de Vico, 1835
sources: Michelet, Principes de la philosophie de l'histoire (1827)
Internet Archive catalogue records, 1827 and 1835 editions

stops.name: A commodius vicus of recirculation
stops.campa: Two centuries on, a book appears in London and New York whose very first sentence carries Vico's name folded into a pun, a commodius vicus of recirculation. James Joyce has built Finnegans Wake, seventeen years in the writing in Paris, on the Neapolitan's wheel of gods, heroes, men, and the ricorso that returns them all to the beginning, and closes the book mid-sentence so that its last words run back into its first. The nation tells its fable again, and again: the wake is a corso that will not stop turning, and Vico, a hundred and ninety-five years dead, is its architect.
stops.quote: riverrun, past Eve and Adam's, from swerve of shore to bend of bay, brings us by a commodius vicus of recirculation back to Howth Castle and Environs.
stops.quote_source: James Joyce, Finnegans Wake (1939), opening sentence
suggested_refs: Finnegans Wake, published 4 May 1939 by Faber and Faber (24 Russell Square, London) and Viking Press (New York), structured on Vico's four-part cycle
sources: Joyce, Finnegans Wake (1939)
